analysis.title: Fed Call Change
key_insights: Stanley adds a third 25 bp Fed hike in March 2027. His prior call was a December 2026 hike and then a hold through 2027. Including the September hike, that makes three quarter-point increases over roughly six months and 75 bp cumulative.

Driver 1, strong economy: Q3 real consumer spending rose 3.8% annualized for a second straight quarter, real business fixed investment rose over 13% annualized, and real domestic demand rose 5.0% annualized, the best since the 2020-21 COVID bounce.

The October payrolls gain was 165K, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, and average hourly earnings rose 0.4%. September hourly earnings were revised from 0.1% to 0.3%. Initial jobless claims have been at or below 200K every week since early September. Wages are now a possible inflation risk.

Fed officials (Williams, Goolsbee, Collins) now say the economy may be overheating. Stanley argues this turns the labor market from a neutral factor into an added inflation risk and a new reason to tighten.

Driver 2, broadening inflation: officials now add AI data-center demand to tariffs and energy as a cause of core inflation. Goolsbee said the demand overheating is 'starting to spread out of its lane.'

Shelter inflation has re-accelerated since April. Rent and owners' equivalent rent rose at annualized rates of 3.4% and 3.8% over the last seven months. The Zillow Rent Index has risen 0.3% or more in each of the past five months. Stanley attributes the earlier softness to the missing October 2025 CPI survey.
Core services ex housing in the PCE deflator rose 0.5% in August and 0.4% in September. The year-over-year rate reached 3.6% in September, up from 3.15% at end-2025 and the highest since late 2024.

The Cleveland Fed median CPI rose 0.3% in October. The 16% trimmed-mean CPI rose from 0.2% in August to 0.3% in September and 0.4% in October. Its year-over-year rate rose a combined three tenths over two months to 2.9%.

Driver 3, higher neutral rate: early in 2026 the FOMC center put neutral near 3%, which made the 3.625% policy rate 'modestly restrictive.' Schmid now calls policy 'fairly accommodative.' Logan puts the funds rate at least 50 bp below modest restriction. Barkin sees policy near neutral. Williams and Daly, who lean dovish, have called for more hikes.
Stanley's earlier call assumed neutral had been revised up about 50 bp to near 3.5%. Officials now appear open to neutral being higher still, and worry about overtightening has faded.

Driver 4, input cost passthrough: Waller cited a Fed Board staff paper finding that ISM commodity price reports predict PPI a few months later, and said October ISM data point to more price increases. Barkin and Daly report firms looking to pass on costs. The October NFIB 'Actual Price Changes' index rose 2 points to +33, and 'Price Plans' rose 6 points to +37, the highest since 2022.

Stanley expects firm inflation over the next three to six months, with possible acceleration. He sees some relief if tariffs are done and oil falls. The IEA said oil supply outpaced demand in October for the first time since the conflict began.

Why not more: Waller floated a 50 bp hike in December and some officials are open to consecutive-meeting moves. Stanley expects the FOMC to keep an every-other-meeting pace. That means a skipped October meeting, a December hike, a skipped January meeting, a March hike, and possibly a fourth hike in June if core inflation stays at or above 3%.

The September FOMC dots put the 2027 median at 4.125% and the high at 4.375%. Stanley says these may be too conservative. He calls the Warsh Fed more serious about fighting inflation, and expects relief by spring. He says he may need to revise again if it does not arrive.

macro_indicators.reading: Hikes of 25 bp in December 2026 and March 2027, after the September 2026 hike, 75 bp cumulative
macro_indicators.interpretation: Stanley moves from one more hike to two more, then a hold. A fourth hike in June 2027 is a risk if core inflation stays at or above 3%.
The report describes this as the policy setting that was once called modestly restrictive. Several officials now call it neutral or accommodative.
Stanley says these may prove somewhat too conservative.

risk_factors: Input cost passthrough could be larger and faster than expected, and inflation could accelerate over the next three to six months.
The economy could overheat across several sectors, including AI data-center demand.
A faster pace of tightening is possible. Waller raised a 50 bp hike in December and some officials are open to consecutive-meeting hikes.
A fourth hike in June 2027 is possible if core inflation stays at or above 3% well into next year.
Neutral could be higher than officials now assume, which would require more tightening.
Relief expected by spring may not arrive. Stanley says he may need to revise again.
geopolitical: The IEA said oil supply outpaced demand in October for the first time since the conflict began. Stanley uses this as a reason oil prices could fall.

tension_points.bull_case: Waller raised the possibility of a 50 bp hike in December, and others are open to acting at consecutive meetings. Neutral may be higher than thought, so faster tightening could be needed.
tension_points.bear_case: Stanley sees a consensus for gradual hikes, citing Barkin, Paulson, Daly and Logan. Logan said slower adjustment helps households and businesses adapt and reduces the risk of a sharper downturn. He expects an every-other-meeting cadence.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If core inflation stays at or above 3% well into 2027 or the economy keeps overheating, a fourth hike in June becomes likely. Relief on prices by spring would end the cycle.
